flawed_step: Step 4: The inference P(A ∩ B) > 1/2 from P(A) > 1/2 and P(B) > 1/2 is invalid; only P(A ∩ B) ≥ P(A)+P(B)-1 > 0 follows.
counterexample: Let X take values 4 and 0 with probabilities 2/3 and 1/3; let Y=3 almost surely; and let Z take values 6 and 2 with probabilities 1/3 and 2/3. Define them mutually independently. Then P(X>Y)=2/3 and P(Y>Z)=2/3, but P(X>Z)=(2/3)(2/3)=4/9.
assessment_summary:
1. Assume X, Y, and Z are mutually independent and that P(X>Y)>1/2 and P(Y>Z)>1/2. — Justified: this states the hypotheses for a proof attempt.
2. Set A={X>Y}, B={Y>Z}, and C={X>Z}. — Justified: these are valid event definitions.
3. A∩B⊆C. — Justified: for real numbers, X>Y and Y>Z imply X>Z pointwise.
4. Claim P(A∩B)>1/2 because P(A)>1/2 and P(B)>1/2. — Not justified: the union bound gives only P(A∩B)≥P(A)+P(B)-1>0. Moreover, A and B need not be independent because both involve Y; even independence would yield only a product greater than 1/4.
5. From Steps 3–4, infer P(C)≥P(A∩B)>1/2. — Not justified: the containment inequality is valid, but the required bound from Step 4 is invalid.
6. Conclude that X beats Z, establishing transitivity. — Not justified: it depends on the invalid Steps 4–5.
7. To determine whether the statement itself is false, take mutually independent variables with P(X=4)=2/3, P(X=0)=1/3; Y=3 almost surely; and P(Z=6)=1/3, P(Z=2)=2/3. — Justified: these are real-valued variables and can be defined on the product probability space, making them mutually independent.
8. P(X>Y)=P(X=4)=2/3>1/2. — Justified: Y is always 3, and precisely X=4 beats it.
9. P(Y>Z)=P(Z=2)=2/3>1/2. — Justified: Y=3 beats Z precisely when Z=2.
10. P(X>Z)=P(X=4,Z=2)=(2/3)(2/3)=4/9≤1/2. — Justified: independence permits multiplication, and this is the only value combination for which X>Z.
11. Thus X beats Y and Y beats Z, while X does not beat Z. — Justified: Steps 8–10 provide a counterexample, so the asserted transitivity is false.
